Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Agikuyu moi kuhitha ndia, matiui kuhitha uhoro
Literal Translation: The Kikuyu know how to conceal their quiver, but do not know how to conceal their secrets.
Explanation: While the Kikuyu are clever at hiding their weapons (intentions or strengths), they are not good at keeping personal or tribal secrets among themselves.
English Equivalent: A man may hide his weapons, but not his heart.

Literal Translation: Two guests (at the same time) have no welcome.
Explanation: It is difficult to properly host and attend to two visitors simultaneously. Hospitality is best given to one at a time.

Literal Translation: Two guests love a different song.
Explanation: Different people have different tastes and needs. You cannot treat two visitors in exactly the same manner because their preferences will differ.
English Equivalent: Every man has his hobby horse.

Literal Translation: He looks after money as the ‘njuu’ looks after locusts.
Explanation: The 'njuu' bird follows swarms of locusts to feed on them incessantly. This refers to a person who is constantly and greedily preoccupied with accumulating wealth.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Aka eri ni nyungu igiri cia utugi
Literal Translation: Two wives are two pots full of poison.
Explanation: Polygamy often leads to jealousy, rivalry, and domestic strife, making a home full of trouble.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Aka matiri cia ndiiro no cia nyiniko
Literal Translation: Women have no upright words, but only crooked ones.
Explanation: A proverb expressing a traditional, patriarchal view that women are not straightforward and cannot keep secrets. (Note: This reflects a specific cultural bias).
English Equivalent: Women conceal all that they know not.

Literal Translation: Wives and oxen have no friends.
Explanation: Certain prized possessions, like wives and valuable livestock, are not to be lent out or shared with friends.
English Equivalent: Love your neighbor, but do not lend him your wife.

Literal Translation: Men are equal when they are going and walking.
Explanation: Differences in social status, wealth, or ability are less noticeable when people are simply traveling together on a road.
English Equivalent: On the long road, all men are equal.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Andu matari ndundu mahuragwo na njuguma imwe
Literal Translation: People who have no secret agreement are beaten by a single club.
Explanation: A group without unity and a common, confidential plan can be easily defeated by a single, determined adversary.

Literal Translation: Men do not know liberality.
Explanation: People rarely give anything without the expectation of something in return.
English Equivalent: One does not give without hope of return.

Literal Translation: Men do not know hard firewood, but only soft wood.
Explanation: People tend to avoid difficult tasks and choose only the easy ones.
English Equivalent: People put aside hard tasks and devote themselves only to easy ones.

Literal Translation: Live men do not lack work.
Explanation: Life is inherently full of challenges and tasks. A living person will always have something to do or some problem to solve.
English Equivalent: Life would be too smooth if it had no rubs.

Literal Translation: He who seeks his goat with the man who ate it, is certain not to find it.
Explanation: Do not expect to find stolen goods in the possession of the thief. Do not seek justice from the one who committed the wrong.
English Equivalent: Do not look for stolen goods in the robber’s house.

Literal Translation: Men have got quills.
Explanation: Do not annoy others, because they have the means and will to retaliate and hurt you.
English Equivalent: Do evil and look for like.

Literal Translation: Necessities never end.
Explanation: Life is a continuous series of needs and troubles.
English Equivalent: He that will have no trouble in this world must not be born in it.

Literal Translation: The elders drink afterwards.
Explanation: Elderly people are patient and not in a hurry, unlike the young. They are content to wait their turn.

Literal Translation: The food found Wacu in the field.
Explanation: From a legend about a despised wife, Wacu, who was overlooked during a feast but was provided for by a raven that brought her meat. It means that God looks after the poor and neglected.
English Equivalent: God takes care of His poor.

Literal Translation: The property of a helpless man must not be divided before his death.
Explanation: A helpless person cannot easily replace what he has, so his possessions should not be distributed among heirs while he is still alive and dependent on them.
English Equivalent: Do not skin the bear before it is killed.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Cia mucii iri gacuguma gacio gatathukagio ni muthuri ungi tiga mwenegwo
Literal Translation: Home affairs have their staff, which cannot be brandished by anyone but the head of the house.
Explanation: Private family matters should be handled only by the head of the household. There should be only one authority in a home.
English Equivalent: Every man is king in his own castle.

Literal Translation: Home affairs must not go into the open.
Explanation: Family problems and private matters should not be discussed in public.
English Equivalent: Do not wash your dirty linen in public.

Literal Translation: Home affairs cannot be told to the public.
Explanation: Similar to the previous proverb, it stresses the importance of keeping family business within the family.
English Equivalent: Do not wash your dirty linen in public.

Literal Translation: The widow’s sons have no tears.
Explanation: Children who have suffered hardship from an early age become accustomed to it and do not show their grief as openly.
English Equivalent: He that is born to sorrow, bears it better.

Literal Translation: Birds agree when flying down, but do not agree when flying up.
Explanation: It is easy for people to agree when starting an enterprise (coming down to feed), but they often quarrel when it's time to share the profits or results (flying up after eating).
English Equivalent: Company in distress makes trouble less.

Literal Translation: Bought things do not fill the granary.
Explanation: You cannot become truly wealthy or self-sufficient merely by purchasing things; you must cultivate your own land and produce your own food.
English Equivalent: Do not hope to become rich without cultivating your fields.

Literal Translation: When there is a shortage of figs, birds eat the fruits of the ‘mugumo’.
Explanation: When preferred resources are scarce, people will make do with what is normally considered inferior or less desirable.
English Equivalent: If thou hast not a capon, feed on an onion.

Literal Translation: The buying of a wife begins from a little thing.
Explanation: Great undertakings, like marriage, start with small, initial steps or payments.
English Equivalent: Great oaks from little acorns grow.

Literal Translation: Goats fall that take hold of lichens.
Explanation: Relying on something weak or insubstantial (like lichens on a rock) for support will lead to failure. Unsatisfactory excuses are an insufficient defence.
English Equivalent: A house built on sand cannot stand.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Cionje ikumi irugitwo ni umwe uri na hinya
Literal Translation: Ten helpless people were surpassed by a single strong person.
Explanation: The quality of one capable person is better than the quantity of many who are weak or ineffective.
English Equivalent: One able man is worth a dozen unable.

Literal Translation: A long lawsuit breeds poverty.
Explanation: Protracted legal disputes consume time and resources, often leading to financial ruin for the parties involved.
English Equivalent: Going to law is losing a cow for the sake of a cat.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Cira munene ni wa uthoni igikua
Literal Translation: The breaking of a betrothal is no small matter.
Explanation: Dissolving a marriage agreement is a serious affair, as it involves the return of substantial bride price payments and has social consequences.
English Equivalent: To break an engagement is a serious business.

Literal Translation: The lawsuit of a fool keeps the court (sitting) all day.
Explanation: A foolish person's case is difficult to resolve because they lack sense, leading to protracted and pointless arguments.
English Equivalent: The lawsuit of a fool never comes to an end.

Literal Translation: Home affairs are not to be carried on in the public square.
Explanation: Private family matters should not be debated or resolved in a public forum.
English Equivalent: Do not wash your dirty linen in public.

Literal Translation: Every case begins from the stomach.
Explanation: Literally, every court case begins with the killing and eating of an animal for the judges. Figuratively, one of the most fundamental concerns in life is securing food.

Literal Translation: We speak by proverb: he who is intelligent will understand.
Explanation: Wise sayings are used to convey truths, and a smart person will grasp the hidden meaning.
English Equivalent: A word to the wise is enough.

Literal Translation: Clear out of the ‘thakirio’.
Explanation: The 'thakirio' is the wife's place in the hut where she distributes food. This is a command to mind your own business and not interfere in another's domain.

Literal Translation: He who spends his time adorning himself knows he is going to a dance.
Explanation: People's actions are purposeful. If someone is preparing elaborately, there is a specific reason for it.
English Equivalent: There is a reason for everything.

Literal Translation: He who adorns himself knows to what sort of dance he is going.
Explanation: Similar to the previous proverb, it emphasizes that preparation is tailored to a specific goal or event.
English Equivalent: There is a reason for everything.

Literal Translation: The fool takes many people with him.
Explanation: A foolish person, when invited somewhere, often brings along uninvited guests, causing inconvenience.
English Equivalent: A fool cannot bear his own company.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Garurira mbeu ti ya kinya kimwe
Literal Translation: Change seeds, taking them from different calabashes.
Explanation: It is beneficial to introduce new blood, new ideas, or new methods rather than sticking to a single source.
English Equivalent: It is good to introduce new blood.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gatami kari mondo yene gatingikurutira wira
Literal Translation: The piece of cloth that is in another’s bag does not patch your garment.
Explanation: You cannot rely on someone else's resources to solve your own problems. What belongs to another is not yours to use.
English Equivalent: You cannot borrow another man's coat.

Literal Translation: A little, contemptible path is sometimes the one that leads you to the highway.
Explanation: A small or humble beginning can lead to great things. Do not despise small opportunities.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gatitu ka muimwo ni iri noko kari miti
Literal Translation: The forest of an unpleasant (ill-liked) person is the one that has trees.
Explanation: Ironically, people who are disliked or considered wicked often prosper and possess valuable things.

Literal Translation: The grove of the heart is not laid open.
Explanation: A person's innermost thoughts and feelings are private and cannot be fully known by others.
English Equivalent: The heart is a hidden forest.

Literal Translation: Nobody cries that has not been pinched.
Explanation: There is always a cause for an effect. An action or complaint does not come from nothing.

Literal Translation: Darkness caused to dance even him who cannot.
Explanation: In the dark, distinctions are blurred. A person's lack of skill or status is hidden, allowing them to participate as if they were capable or equal.
English Equivalent: All cats are grey in the dark.

Literal Translation: A secret agreement enabled people to kill Watatua.
Explanation: Watatua was a powerful chief who was killed through a secret plot, as he was invincible in open combat. Secrecy and conspiracy can overcome brute strength.

Literal Translation: A market can be spoilt by one woman.
Explanation: The misconduct or trouble caused by a single person can ruin an event or a community's effort.
English Equivalent: One ill weed mars a whole pot of pottage.

Literal Translation: Every feast has its guest of honour.
Explanation: In every gathering or event, there is someone who holds a position of importance or respect.
English Equivalent: Every feast has its chief guest.

Literal Translation: One appointment is eaten by another.
Explanation: Today's plans or events are replaced or overshadowed by those of tomorrow. The present consumes the past.

Literal Translation: That of circumcision is a hard appointment.
Explanation: The Kikuyu circumcision rite is a painful but necessary transition into adulthood. It signifies that important achievements often require enduring hardship.

Literal Translation: A Kikuyu always seeks his own things.
Explanation: People naturally pursue their own interests and care for what belongs to them.

Literal Translation: A Kikuyu’s things are shared with his mother.
Explanation: Family bonds are strong, and one shares what they have with close relatives.

Literal Translation: A Kikuyu’s things are tied to his land.
Explanation: Property and land are closely linked; what you own is often connected to the land you cultivate or inhabit.

Literal Translation: A Kikuyu does things with love.
Explanation: Actions done with genuine care and affection are more successful and meaningful.
English Equivalent: Do things with love and dedication.

Literal Translation: A Kikuyu is known by his speech in council.
Explanation: A person’s character and wisdom are revealed by how they speak in public or in leadership positions.

Literal Translation: A Kikuyu’s word is heavy.
Explanation: A Kikuyu keeps promises and their word carries weight; they are trustworthy.
English Equivalent: A man’s word is his bond.

Literal Translation: A Kikuyu fears no obstacle.
Explanation: Bravery and determination are valued; a strong person faces challenges without fear.

Literal Translation: A Kikuyu who owns a path is guided.
Explanation: Those with initiative and leadership provide direction for others.
English Equivalent: He who leads paves the way.

Literal Translation: A Kikuyu is a home builder.
Explanation: They invest in family, shelter, and community, emphasizing stability and roots.
English Equivalent: Home is where the heart is.

Literal Translation: A Kikuyu does what is done with deep love.
Explanation: Care and affection bring success to all endeavours.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthaka kĩa mũno kĩarĩa na mbeca
Literal Translation: A fertile land brings wealth.
Explanation: Productivity and hard work in good land leads to prosperity.
English Equivalent: The land that yields well makes a wealthy man.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthaka kĩa mũno kĩarĩa na maũndũ
Literal Translation: A fertile land grows many things.
Explanation: Good resources allow for multiple benefits; diversity in output is valuable.

Literal Translation: The land of love brings wealth.
Explanation: Land that is cultivated with care and dedication produces abundance.

Literal Translation: The hill of love brings wealth.
Explanation: Effort and dedication in one’s endeavors lead to reward.

Literal Translation: A hill of love knows no obstacles.
Explanation: Dedication and affection overcome difficulties.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩarĩa na mbeca
Literal Translation: A hill of love bears wealth.
Explanation: Efforts done with care yield material and emotional rewards.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩarĩa na wendo
Literal Translation: A hill of love begets love.
Explanation: Acts of care and dedication attract more care in return.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩarĩa na kĩhoto
Literal Translation: A hill of love bears humility.
Explanation: True love and dedication teach humility and respect.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩa mũno kĩa mbeca
Literal Translation: A hill of great love yields wealth.
Explanation: Strong dedication and care produce significant rewards.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩa mũno kĩa wendo
Literal Translation: A hill of great love brings love.
Explanation: Intense care and dedication attract affection and loyalty.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩa mũno kĩa kĩhoto
Literal Translation: A hill of great love bears humility.
Explanation: True greatness in love brings modesty and gentleness.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩa mũno kĩa mũno
Literal Translation: A hill of great love brings greatness.
Explanation: Dedication and care elevate people to prominence.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩa mũno kĩa thutha
Literal Translation: A hill of great love overcomes obstacles.
Explanation: Dedication, love, and effort can surmount difficulties.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩa mũno kĩa mũciĩ
Literal Translation: A hill of great love produces fruit.
Explanation: Devotion and effort yield tangible results.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩa mũno kĩa mũno kĩarĩa na wendo
Literal Translation: A hill of great love brings love and greatness.
Explanation: Dedication and care create both respect and prosperity.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩa mũno kĩa mũno kĩa mũciĩ
Literal Translation: A hill of great love brings greatness and fruit.
Explanation: Strong dedication results in both esteem and tangible achievements.
English Equivalent: Great effort yields both honor and reward.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Gĩthima kĩa wendo kĩa mũno kĩa mũno kĩa mũciĩ kĩarĩa na mbeca
Literal Translation: A hill of great love brings greatness, fruit, and wealth.
Explanation: Devotion and effort lead to respect, tangible results, and prosperity.
English Equivalent: Great love and effort bring honor, reward, and wealth.

Literal Translation: There is no perfect helper.
Explanation: No one can provide complete help; everyone has limitations.

Literal Translation: There is nothing great without effort.
Explanation: Achievement requires work and perseverance.

Literal Translation: Nothing is hidden forever.
Explanation: Secrets or truth will eventually be revealed.

Literal Translation: Nothing is more powerful than effort.
Explanation: Dedication and hard work achieve what seems impossible.

Literal Translation: There is no perfect helper.
Explanation: Everyone can fail; reliance on others is never complete.

Literal Translation: No helper is infallible.
Explanation: Helpers have limitations; one should also rely on themselves.

Literal Translation: Nothing is greater than what is eaten.
Explanation: Basic needs and sustenance are paramount.

Literal Translation: There is no great child.
Explanation: Children need guidance and cannot succeed without direction.

Literal Translation: No love is perfect.
Explanation: Love always involves compromise, challenges, or limitations.

Literal Translation: There is no perfect council.
Explanation: Advice and leadership may be wise but never flawless.
English Equivalent: Even the best advice has limits.

Literal Translation: Nothing is greater than effort.
Explanation: Effort is the key to success in any endeavor.

Literal Translation: No child is without learning.
Explanation: Every child has the potential to grow and gain knowledge.

Literal Translation: There is no learning without a child.
Explanation: Learning often comes through practice and guidance.

Literal Translation: There is no beloved child.
Explanation: All children require equal attention; favoritism is harmful.

Literal Translation: No love is without effort.
Explanation: True affection requires care and attention.

Literal Translation: No helper is flawless.
Explanation: Helpers have limitations; one should also rely on themselves.

Literal Translation: No helper acts with pure love.
Explanation: Assistance is often mixed with personal motives or limits.

Literal Translation: No love exists without effort.
Explanation: All meaningful relationships require work.

Literal Translation: No child is without love.
Explanation: Children are naturally cared for, even if imperfectly.
English Equivalent: Every child is loved in some way.

Literal Translation: Nothing happens without a challenge.
Explanation: All accomplishments require effort and overcoming obstacles.

Literal Translation: There is no perfect helper for a child.
Explanation: Children need multiple forms of guidance; no single helper suffices.
English Equivalent: It takes a village to raise a child.

Literal Translation: No child is without difficulty.
Explanation: Raising children comes with challenges.
English Equivalent: Children bring both joy and trouble.

Literal Translation: No effort is without difficulty.
Explanation: All endeavors come with challenges that must be faced.

Literal Translation: No helper comes without difficulty.
Explanation: Even those who assist have limitations or create challenges.

Literal Translation: No child grows without challenges.
Explanation: Growth and learning often occur through overcoming difficulties.

Literal Translation: No child receives love perfectly.
Explanation: Even the most cared-for child experiences hardship.

Literal Translation: No child avoids challenges.
Explanation: Challenges are inevitable in life, even for the young.

Literal Translation: No child learns without effort.
Explanation: Children must actively participate to gain knowledge.

Literal Translation: There is no great child.
Explanation: True greatness comes with guidance, experience, and effort.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Haria hari ũhoro, ti haria hari ndeto
Literal Translation: Where there is truth, there is no need for many words.
Explanation: The truth is simple and self-evident and does not require lengthy arguments or persuasion.

Literal Translation: One step does not find the way.
Explanation: You must take continuous steps and persist to reach your goal; success is not achieved by a single action.
English Equivalent: One swallow does not make a summer.

Literal Translation: Patience finishes great things.
Explanation: Great achievements are realized through perseverance and tolerance, not haste.

Literal Translation: The pit eats what is in it.
Explanation: If you keep silent about a problem or secret, it will consume you or cause trouble (like a person or thing falling into an unmarked pit).
English Equivalent: A burden shared is a burden halved.

Literal Translation: Ten fools are surpassed by one wise man.
Explanation: Quality of thought and wisdom trumps the mere quantity of people; collective foolishness is useless.
English Equivalent: A handful of common sense is worth a bushel of learning.

Literal Translation: A fool is found quarreling with the garden (field).
Explanation: A foolish person quarrels with the inevitable consequences of their own actions or laziness, such as a poor harvest.
English Equivalent: The fault is not in our stars, but in ourselves.

Literal Translation: Weight has no special tree (stick) for lifting.
Explanation: Any problem, regardless of how big or small, requires appropriate effort to solve it; there is no special shortcut.
English Equivalent: A problem is a problem, no matter its size.

Literal Translation: That which has no person (owner) has no defense.
Explanation: An orphan, or someone without protection or friends, is easily taken advantage of. Protection comes from one's social ties.
English Equivalent: The lonely sheep is the wolf's prey.

Literal Translation: That which has no love has no person.
Explanation: A life or endeavor without dedication, care, or affection is meaningless or will fail to attract support.
English Equivalent: All labor is lost that is not for love.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Ithatũ rĩtari ndeto nĩrĩo rĩrũgĩte mũkĩro
Literal Translation: A visit without words (talk) is better than a greeting (from afar).
Explanation: Physical presence and direct interaction are more valuable than mere formality or distant acknowledgment.

Literal Translation: One sacrifice does not save another.
Explanation: Each problem or debt must be addressed individually. You cannot use a single effort or payment to cover multiple obligations.
English Equivalent: Pay your debts one by one.

Literal Translation: Truth (Justice) is found with the elder.
Explanation: Wisdom and impartiality, necessary for true justice, reside with the experienced elders who preside over the court (kiama).

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Kĩhumo kĩa mũndũ nĩ mũciĩ wake
Literal Translation: The origin (background) of a person is his home.
Explanation: A person's character, manners, and reputation are strongly influenced by the family and home from which they come.
English Equivalent: The apple does not fall far from the tree.

Literal Translation: The fully completed thing is found to have been a story.
Explanation: When a difficult project is finished, the hardship is forgotten, and it becomes a mere memory or tale.

Literal Translation: One debt on another found it to be a story (a mere report).
Explanation: If you incur debt after debt, eventually the creditors will talk about it, and the accumulated debt will become a public, embarrassing affair.
English Equivalent: He that goes a borrowing, goes a sorrowing.

Literal Translation: The basket only sees what is in it.
Explanation: A person can only act or speak based on the knowledge they possess. Be content with your own capability and resources.

Literal Translation: That basket was a home.
Explanation: A small basket (kĩondo) often holds a person's most essential possessions, hence, it is a symbol of self-sufficiency and resourcefulness.

Literal Translation: A basket that is at home has no difficulty.
Explanation: When one is secure and cared for in their own home, they are safe from the challenges of the outside world.
English Equivalent: There is no place like home.

Literal Translation: That which was finished is the one that is started.
Explanation: When a task fails, you must begin again from the point of failure. Also: an old habit or problem often resurfaces.

Literal Translation: That which goes is the one that is at home.
Explanation: Your true property is what you have with you (what you have earned or carry), not what you left behind.
English Equivalent: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.

Literal Translation: A fool in the garden has a lesson.
Explanation: Even a foolish person, through personal experience and mistakes (like a poor harvest), will eventually learn a lesson.

Literal Translation: A fool with many words is the one that is despised.
Explanation: A foolish person who talks too much exposes their lack of sense and earns contempt.

Literal Translation: A fool in the clan has no home.
Explanation: A person who constantly brings trouble or shame to their family will eventually be ostracized or disowned.
English Equivalent: A black sheep spoils the flock.

Literal Translation: A fool who loves has difficulty.
Explanation: If an unwise person tries to show affection, they often mess things up, causing more trouble than good.
English Equivalent: Love does not conquer all for a fool.

Literal Translation: To conceal a word is to speak it.
Explanation: An important secret that is kept inside will eventually affect one's actions or behavior, revealing itself indirectly.
English Equivalent: The hidden thought changes the deed.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Kũnyita nyama ya ng'ombe gĩkũrũ nĩ kũiyũkĩa
Literal Translation: To hold the meat of a cow by the neck is to lift it.
Explanation: You must address a problem directly and at its source if you wish to solve it. Tackle the head of the issue.

Literal Translation: To stand up for oneself is to speak.
Explanation: Defending one's rights or position requires vocal and assertive action.
English Equivalent: If you don’t stand for something, you’ll fall for anything.

Literal Translation: To eat the garden is to eat words.
Explanation: If you misuse or deplete communal resources (the garden), you will soon be subject to criticism and legal reprimand (words in court).
English Equivalent: Misuse of resources leads to accountability.

Literal Translation: To flee is to flee.
Explanation: Once you have decided to flee from danger, do not look back or hesitate; commit fully to your escape.
English Equivalent: He that will not fight, may fly.

Literal Translation: Affairs have standing (a place to stand).
Explanation: All matters or actions have consequences that will remain long after the deed is done. Nothing is truly fleeting.

Literal Translation: Money is a quarrel.
Explanation: Wealth often brings dispute, envy, and conflict among friends and family.
English Equivalent: Money is the root of all evil.

Literal Translation: A field without an old man (owner) is easy.
Explanation: Land that is neglected or has no firm owner is easily taken over or cultivated by others.

Literal Translation: One clan has no fullness (completeness).
Explanation: No single family or clan is self-sufficient. Society thrives on interdependence between different groups (e.g., through marriage or trade).

Literal Translation: A field without love has no child.
Explanation: A piece of land that is not cultivated with care and dedication will yield no harvest (no 'child'/fruit).
English Equivalent: A little tillage is a great tillage.

Literal Translation: A person without a home has no clan.
Explanation: A person without stable family life or community ties loses their identity and social support.
English Equivalent: A rolling stone gathers no moss.

Literal Translation: A person of words is a clan.
Explanation: A person who is knowledgeable and articulate can influence many people, acting as a representative or leader for their whole community.
English Equivalent: The pen is mightier than the sword.

Literal Translation: A person without love is easy (to exploit).
Explanation: A lonely or loveless person lacks emotional support and is vulnerable to manipulation or exploitation.
English Equivalent: The unloved is easily led astray.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Mũndũ wĩ mũno nĩ kĩrĩa kĩarĩ rũgano
Literal Translation: A great person is one who was once a story.
Explanation: Greatness is not born overnight; it is the result of a long journey and many past deeds that eventually become tales.
English Equivalent: Greatness is a journey, not a destination.

Literal Translation: A person’s son has no lesson (to be taught from afar).
Explanation: Children must be taught directly and personally; generalized advice is often insufficient.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Mũrũ wa mũndũ ũtarĩ ũhoro nĩ mũciĩ
Literal Translation: A person's son who has no lesson is a child (immature).
Explanation: A child who has not been taught discipline and wisdom remains childish and unprepared for life.
English Equivalent: A child left to himself brings shame to his mother.

Literal Translation: A field without love has no difficulty.
Explanation: If you don't care about a piece of land, you won't suffer or put in effort, leading to a poor result.

Literal Translation: A person's relative has no home (of their own).
Explanation: A close relative is always welcome in your home, implying that kinship transcends ownership and boundaries.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Ndugu ya mũndũ ĩthiaga na mũndũ
Literal Translation: A person's relative goes with the person.
Explanation: Your true family and friends remain with you regardless of your circumstance or location.
English Equivalent: Friendship follows the man, not the man the friendship.

Literal Translation: It is justice that was a home.
Explanation: A stable and just home environment is the foundation for proper growth and wisdom.
English Equivalent: A just home is a good home.

Proverb (Gĩkũyũ): Nĩ kĩrĩa gĩathirire nĩkĩo kĩarĩ wendo
Literal Translation: That which was finished is the one that was loved.
Explanation: We often realize the value of something only after it is lost or finished.
English Equivalent: Absence makes the heart grow fonder.

Literal Translation: It is a home that is not great (perfect).
Explanation: Every family or home has its flaws and imperfections, yet it remains important.

Literal Translation: The path of truth is difficult.
Explanation: Telling the truth and pursuing justice often involves facing challenges and conflict.
English Equivalent: The road to truth is rough.

Literal Translation: Meat without love is only one (worthless).
Explanation: A gift given without sincerity or affection loses its value, no matter how substantial it is.
English Equivalent: A gift without a heart is a bare present.

Literal Translation: The meat of the child has no love.
Explanation: A child's gift (meat from their share) is given without guile or expectation of return, making it pure, though perhaps small.
English Equivalent: A child's gift is given freely.

Literal Translation: One lesson has no child (it is not complete).
Explanation: A single piece of advice or experience is not enough; comprehensive learning requires continuous teaching and practice.

Literal Translation: One lesson is great (important).
Explanation: Even a small piece of knowledge or wisdom can be profoundly impactful if absorbed correctly.
English Equivalent: A small spark can light a great fire.

Literal Translation: One lesson has a child (it can teach).
Explanation: Every experience, even a singular one, holds a valuable lesson that can shape future behavior.
English Equivalent: There is a lesson in everything.

Literal Translation: A person's truth has no home (it travels).
Explanation: A person's reputation and character follow them wherever they go; truth cannot be confined to one place.

Literal Translation: A person's truth has love.
Explanation: Sincerity and honesty (truth) in one's character attract respect and affection.

Literal Translation: A person's truth has difficulty.
Explanation: Telling the truth can be hard and may lead to negative consequences or conflicts.

Literal Translation: A person's truth is great.
Explanation: A person of integrity is highly valued and respected in the community.

Literal Translation: A person's simplicity is a home.
Explanation: A simple, humble person attracts others and creates a welcoming environment, like a warm home.

Literal Translation: A person's simplicity is a lesson.
Explanation: Humble and straightforward people teach others the value of avoiding complexity and vanity.

Literal Translation: A person's simplicity is love.
Explanation: A simple heart is a loving heart; lack of pretense makes affection genuine.

Literal Translation: A person's simplicity is difficulty.
Explanation: A person who is too simple or naive can easily be taken advantage of, leading to personal hardship.

Literal Translation: A person's simplicity is great.
Explanation: In certain contexts, humbleness and lack of pretension are considered marks of great character.

Literal Translation: A person's simplicity has no home.
Explanation: An extremely humble person may be too easily overlooked or lack the stability of a defined status.

Literal Translation: The path's truth is great.
Explanation: Experience gained from journeying and confronting the outside world is extremely valuable.

Literal Translation: Great work is a home.
Explanation: A person's dedicated labor and effort create stability and security, much like a home provides shelter.

Literal Translation: Great work is a lesson.
Explanation: Hard, consistent work is the best way to learn skills and gain true wisdom.

Literal Translation: Great work is love.
Explanation: Only deep dedication and love for the task can sustain the effort required for great accomplishments.

Literal Translation: Great work is difficulty.
Explanation: Any highly significant achievement will necessarily involve significant challenges and hardship.
English Equivalent: Great efforts lead to great challenges.

Literal Translation: Great work is great.
Explanation: Hard work and dedication are inherently valuable and lead to admirable results.

Literal Translation: One task has no home.
Explanation: A single, isolated act of labor does not create lasting security; effort must be continuous.

Literal Translation: One task is a lesson.
Explanation: Every completed task, no matter how small, offers some new knowledge or experience.

Literal Translation: One task is love.
Explanation: Even a small act done with affection is valuable.
English Equivalent: A little kindness goes a long way.

Literal Translation: One task is difficulty.
Explanation: Even the simplest task can present unexpected problems.
English Equivalent: Nothing is as easy as it looks.

Literal Translation: One task is great.
Explanation: Focusing intently on a single task can lead to mastery and significant achievement.

Literal Translation: A person's work has no home.
Explanation: The results of one's labor are universal and benefit others outside the immediate family or community.

Literal Translation: A person's work has a lesson.
Explanation: You can always learn from observing or performing someone else's labor.

Literal Translation: A person's work has love.
Explanation: The quality of work reflects the dedication and care put into it.

Literal Translation: A person's work has difficulty.
Explanation: All labor, no matter who performs it, involves inherent challenges.

Literal Translation: A person's work is great.
Explanation: The effort and dedication of a skilled individual are highly esteemed.

Literal Translation: A person's work has no lesson (it is self-evident).
Explanation: The quality of the outcome is the only lesson needed; the results speak for themselves.
English Equivalent: The proof of the pudding is in the eating.

Literal Translation: A person's work has no love (it is impartial).
Explanation: Work should be judged on its merit, not on the personal feelings of the worker or the recipient.
English Equivalent: Judge the work, not the worker.

Literal Translation: A person's work has no difficulty (it is well-executed).
Explanation: When a skilled person works, they make even the most complex task appear easy.

Literal Translation: A person's work is not great (it is just enough).
Explanation: A humble perspective on one's own labor; focus on function rather than boasting.
English Equivalent: Do not boast of your work.

Literal Translation: The work of a lesson is a home.
Explanation: Applying wisdom and learning creates a stable and secure life (a 'home').

Literal Translation: The work of a lesson is love.
Explanation: Caring about one's education and applying the lessons learned demonstrates self-respect and love for life.
English Equivalent: Knowledge is a sign of self-care.

Literal Translation: The work of a lesson is difficulty.
Explanation: The process of acquiring knowledge and understanding is rarely easy; it requires struggle.
English Equivalent: The path of learning is hard.

Literal Translation: The work of a lesson is great.
Explanation: The pursuit of knowledge is a most noble and rewarding endeavor.

Literal Translation: The work of a lesson has no home.
Explanation: Wisdom is not confined to one place; it can be applied universally.

Literal Translation: The work of a lesson has no love (it is objective).
Explanation: Knowledge is neutral; it should be taught and used impartially.

Literal Translation: The work of a lesson has no difficulty (it flows naturally).
Explanation: Once a concept is truly mastered, applying it becomes second nature.

Literal Translation: The work of a lesson is not great (it is fundamental).
Explanation: Basic education is a necessity, not a luxury to be boasted about.

Literal Translation: The work of love is a home.
Explanation: Actions motivated by love and care create stability, warmth, and belonging.
English Equivalent: Love makes a house a home.

Literal Translation: The work of love is difficulty.
Explanation: Maintaining loving relationships often requires great sacrifice and effort.

Literal Translation: The work of love is great.
Explanation: Love is a powerful force that leads to noble deeds and great resilience.

Literal Translation: The work of love has no home.
Explanation: Love is universal and not confined to a single place or family.
